Worth remembering (for general consumption) that minimizing the AIC is in fact asymptotically equivalent to leave-one-out cross-validation (this was demonstrated back in the late 70's). In a similar vein, the BIC (which some people prefer) is asymptotically equivalent to leave-k-out cross-validation when k=n(1-1/(log(n)-1).

Choosing penalty value in occuMulti
Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com>: Jan 12 01:29PM -0500

Hi,
 
The answer to your first question is the optimizePenalty() function included in unmarked. It uses K-fold cross validation to determine which penalty is best from a set of possible penalties you provide. See ?optimizePenalty.
 
If you are comparing across multiple models and including penalties, you should not use AIC (which itself is a form of penalized likelihood). Instead you can use the same cross validation approach used by optimizePenalty for each combination of model and penalty term, and then choose the model/penalty combination with the highest overall cross validation score. Unfortunately unmarked does not have a built in function to do this specific task at the moment. I wrote a small function that returns the CV scores so they can be compared across models. See example below.
 
Thanks to Chris Rota for his input on this question.
 
Ken
 
----------
 
# Run first part of example in occuMulti help (?occuMulti) to get this fitted model
fit
 
set.seed(123)
 
# Find best value of penalty for a single model and re-fit the model with that penalty
# Uses k-fold cross validation
fit_opt <- optimizePenalty(fit, penalties=c(0,1,2))
 
# Compare models
 
# Fit a second model
newocc <- rep("~1", 7)
fit2 <- update(fit, stateformulas=newocc)
 
# Function to extract cross-validation score for each penalty value
# To get the CV score:
# 1. the dataset is divided into K folds of test/train data
# 2. For each fold, fit model with train data and penalty term
# 3. Using fitted coefficients from this model, calculate the sum of the site log-likelihoods for the test data
# 4. Sum across all K folds = final score (higher is better)
get_crossval <- function(object, penalties, k=5){
folds <- unmarked:::partitionKfold(object, k)
 
cvp <- sapply(penalties, function(p, k, fit, folds){
cv <- sapply(1:k, function(i){
refit <- update(fit, data=folds[[i]]$trainData, penalty=p, se=FALSE)
sum(unmarked:::occuMultiLogLik(refit, folds[[i]]$testData))
})
sum(cv)
}, k=k, fit=object, folds=folds)
data.frame(model=deparse(substitute(object)), penalty=penalties, value=cvp)
}
 
# Get CV scores for a range of penalty values for each model
fit_scores <- get_crossval(fit, penalties=c(0,1,2), k=5)
fit2_scores <- get_crossval(fit2, penalties=c(0,1,2), k=5)
 
# Combine and sort. Max CV score = top model
# In this case for a given model the penalties all give very similar
# CV scores - not surprising since these simulated data don't really require penalized likelihood
results <- rbind(fit_scores, fit2_scores)
results[rev(order(results$value)),]
